draft.title: Origin, content, context and purpose
card: Origin
who made the source and when. This tells you how close the maker was to the events.
Content
what the source shows or says, such as the people, objects or events in it.
Context
what was happening at the time it was made, such as the beliefs, rulers or events of the period.
Purpose
why the source was made and who it was meant for. A source made to praise a ruler may leave out their failures.
draft.remember: Ask four questions of a source: who and when, what, what else was happening, and why.

a.q: A historian asks, "Why was this statue of a king made, and who was it meant to impress?" Which part of the source is she looking at?
a.why: Asking why a source was made and who it was meant for is about its purpose. Origin is different: it asks who made it and when, not the reason it was made.
a.clue: Think about the reason the maker had.

b.q: A carving made for a pharaoh shows him defeating many enemies in battle. A student says the carving proves the pharaoh never lost a battle. Which question would best test this claim?
opts: Why was it made, and for whom?
What objects are shown in the carving?
What colour was the stone used?
b.why: A carving made for a ruler may be meant to praise him, so it may leave out defeats. Asking about its purpose tests the claim. Asking what is shown only describes the content and does not explain why defeats might be missing.
b.clue: A source made to praise someone may not tell the whole story.

b.best: Why was it made, and for whom?

problems.detail: Two distractors ('How big is the carving?', 'What colour was the stone used?') are not any of the four questions on the card and cannot test the claim. The right option is the only one about why the source was made, and the clue ('A source made to praise someone…') points straight to it. A student can pick it without knowing the idea. 'What colour was the stone used?' is also awkwardly worded.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate and clear. In question b the distractors are too weak and the clue gives the answer away, so it barely tests the idea of purpose.
